This paper shows the ideas of “neurodiversity” and the “neurodiversity approaches” towards disability and covers how confusion about the meaning of these ideas worsens debate and conflict around the neurodiversity approaches. For example, some say the neurodiversity approaches focus only on society and reject contributions of individual traits to disability (a disputed view), while this paper joins other literature in recognizing the contributions of both individual and society to disability.

One main area of study in developmental science is atypical development: the study of so-called “neurodevelopmental disorders” such as autism or intellectual disability, as well as the growth of mental health challenges and more. Research about atypical development has usually been done within the frame of the medical model, which assumes that disabilities are pathological in nature: that they are medical diseases and disorders of the body and mind which make people have shortfalls and face functional limits.

In this model, the proper response to disability is to try to change disabled people into able-bodied and typically developing people. Though the medical model has long been main in shaping views of disability, it has often been badly received in disability communities (Constantino, 2018; Ne'eman, 2010; Oliver, 1990). Disabled people can find its focus on cure and normalizing annoying when they may not be able, or willing, to change themselves into typically developing, “normal” people.

This paper also covers other disagreements about neurodiversity, such as uncertainty about the range of the approaches − to whom do they apply? − and their effects on diagnostic categories. Finally, it gives advice for developmental researchers who want to do neurodiversity-aligned research. Scholars should study both individual neurodivergent people and the contexts around them. They should consider both strengths and weaknesses. They should recognize their own biases. And they should listen to and learn from neurodivergent people.
Keywords: Social model, Medical model, Disability, Neurodevelopmental disabilities, Autism
